title: From Struggling (With) Screening Tests to Mouse Models of Depression‐Relevant Neurobehavioral States
author: Pryce
materials: Although attempts to design a rodent model of “depression‐like state” were and will always be unrealistic, there will inevitably be pressure to do so for as long as the focus of psychiatric research is on the heterogenous, nosological entity of MDD. This is one of the major reasons why it is so important that relatively recent initiatives have redirected research focus away from nosological psychiatric entities and toward specific neurobehavioral functions and the pathologies thereof. Such an approach renders neuropsychiatric disorder symptoms and states amenable to study using the methods of molecular, cellular, systems, and behavioral neuroscience; this includes human studies, animal studies, and (back‐)translation between them. Pioneering in this regard have been the Research Domain Criteria (RDoC) framework of the U.S. National Institute of Mental Health (www.nimh.nih.gov) and also, more recently, the Precision Psychiatry Roadmap of the European College of Neuropsychopharmacology (Kas et al., 2025). In the case of the RDoC framework, six domains of psychological/neurobiological processes are identified, with those of most and equable relevance to MDD being negative valence systems and positive valence systems. Negative valence systems are responsible for the processing of aversive events/stimuli, which include acute actual threats, acute potential threats, and chronic exposure to acute and/or potential threats, and the responsiveness to and learning about such events/stimuli. With respect to MDD symptoms, these systems interface with the core symptom of depressed mood (APA, 2013). Furthermore, chronic exposure to acute and/or potential threats, and particularly those that are (perceived as) uncontrollable, is a major etiological risk factor for the onset and maintenance of MDD (Kendler et al., 1999; Pizzagalli, 2014; Sanacora et al., 2022). Positive valence systems are responsible for the processing of rewarding events/stimuli, and include reward anticipation/motivation, learning, valuation, and responsiveness with pleasure. These symptoms interface with the core MDD symptom of diminished interest or pleasure in daily activities (APA, 2013).

steps.title: House experimental and aggressor mice
steps.instruction: Obtain young‑adult male C57BL/6J mice as subjects and aggressive‑dominant male CD‑1 ex‑breeder mice as stressors; house each pair in a cage equipped with a perforated central divider that permits olfactory, auditory and visual contact but prevents tactile contact.

steps.title: House control littermates
steps.instruction: House control C57BL/6J mice in age‑ and weight‑matched littermate pairs without a divider; maintain them under standard colony conditions.

steps.title: Day‑1 attack session
steps.instruction: Place the C57BL/6J mouse and a CD‑1 mouse on the same side of the divider; allow the CD‑1 mouse to attack the C57BL/6J mouse until a cumulative total of 60 seconds of attack is reached or a maximum of 10 minutes elapses, whichever occurs first; then separate the animals by the divider.

steps.title: Maintain distal interaction
steps.instruction: After the attack period, keep the two mice separated by the perforated divider for the remainder of the 24‑hour period, allowing only olfactory, auditory and visual cues.

steps.title: Rotate stressor daily for 15 days
steps.instruction: Each 24‑hour period, move the C57BL/6J mouse to the home cage of a different CD‑1 aggressor and repeat the attack‑then‑separation procedure; continue this rotation for a total of 15 consecutive days to provide chronic social stress.

steps.title: Post‑stress housing before testing
steps.instruction: After the 15‑day CSS protocol, keep each C57BL/6J mouse in its cage with the CD‑1 mouse separated by the divider, without further attacks, throughout the subsequent behavioral testing period.

steps.title: Pavlovian aversion learning (PAL)
steps.instruction: Between 1 day and 5–6 days after completion of the CSS protocol, place each mouse in the conditioning arena (context); present a tone (conditioned stimulus) paired with a mild foot shock to the paws (unconditioned stimulus) for six CS‑US pairings; record freezing behavior during each CS presentation.

steps.title: Optional escitalopram treatment
steps.instruction: If evaluating drug efficacy, administer escitalopram sub‑chronically for 10 days between the PAL session and the subsequent memory test (dose and route follow standard practice, as not specified in the source).

steps.title: Pavlovian aversion memory (PAM)
steps.instruction: Return mice to the same context; first measure baseline (contextual) freezing; then present CS trials without shock and record freezing during each CS; compare the percentage of time spent freezing between CSS‑exposed and control mice.
